questions.question: 23. Physicians are reluctant to prescribe beta-lactam antibiotics to patients with a documented penicillin allergy on their chart.

parts.text: What are four clinical markers of a Type I / IgE-mediated reaction? (2)
What is antigenic component of cross-reactivity between penicillin and cephalosporin? (1)
If the patient had a Stevens-Johnsons reaction to penicillin in the past, can you use penicillin again? Under what circumstances? (1)

cohort_answer.text: Markers: immediate or accelerated onset (30 min-1 hr, rarely 6-48hrs), pruritus and urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis. Cross-reactivity component: R1 side chain. SJS history: avoid use of any beta-lactams in a patient with history of SJS/TEN/severe cutaneous adverse reactions to another beta-lactam; severe disease and lack of alternatives may warrant rechallenge via carefully designed incremental drug challenge with frequent monitoring

questions.question: Patient had immediate hypersensitivity reaction to ampicillin. Major and minor determinant allergy testing for Penicillin was negative. Oral Penicillin challenge testing was negative – (2019)

parts.text: What is the reason there is a reaction to ampicillin, but not to penicillin?
Name one MOST common used abx you should avoid?

cohort_answer.text: Reason: Different R1 side chain, still high risk for cross reaction but not 100%. Avoid: Avoid amoxicillin (almost the same)

questions.question: Beta lactams

parts.text: Mechanism of action?
What's the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?
Given this, what is a way to administer the drug that would make it more effective?
What percentage of patients who say they have a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting the transpeptidase (cross-linking) step of peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis, which activates autolysins and causes bacterial cell lysis (bactericidal).
b) The main pharmacodynamic parameter is time above the MIC (fT>MIC) - beta-lactams display time-dependent killing.
c) Way to maximize effectiveness: administer by extended or continuous infusion (or more frequent dosing) rather than rapid bolus, to maximize the proportion of the dosing interval that free drug concentration remains above the MIC.
d) Only about 10% of patients who report a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test (i.e., roughly 90% test negative, and true IgE-mediated allergy is uncommon).
questions.beyond_mandell: Time-above-MIC PD target and infusion strategy are established PK/PD pharmacology, and the ~10% positive skin-test figure reflects broader penicillin-allergy literature beyond this chapter excerpt.

questions.question: 19) Pt recently had Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction to ampicillin. A skin test is done with major and minor determinants, which is negative. An oral challenge with Penicillin is also negative.

parts.text: What is the most likely explanation for this?
What is one other drug you should counsel this patient to avoid, other than amoxicillin?

cohort_answer.text: Ampicillin had a different R1-side chain from penicillin. Ampicillin has a side chain identical to that of first-generation cephalosporins cephalexin and cefadroxil, and to cefaclor (2nd gen cephalosporin) - avoid these (NOT cefazolin).

questions.question: Beta lactams.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action
What PD parameter is important for these?
What is a way to administer these to take advantage of this PD parameter
What percentage of people who report penicillin allergy will have a negative skin test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: binding of PBPs, inhibiting peptidoglycan transpeptidase cross-linking, leading to cell wall failure and bacterial lysis.
b) Key PD parameter: time above MIC (fT>MIC) - time-dependent bactericidal activity.
c) Administration strategy: prolonged or continuous infusion to maximize time above MIC.
d) Approximately 90% of people who report a penicillin allergy will have a negative skin test.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ~90% negative skin-test figure reflects established penicillin-allergy epidemiology beyond this excerpt.

questions.question: Physicians are more likely to prescribe non-beta lactam antibiotics to patients who carry a penicillin allergy. The following question examines cephalosporin use in the context of penicillin allergy.

parts.text: What are FOUR symptoms/manifestations of IgE mediated allergic reaction?
What is the antigenic component that causes cross-reactivity between beta-lactams?
If your patient had a previous history of SJS/TENs with penicillin, would you prescribe a cephalosporin? If so, under what circumstances?

questions.model_answer: a) Four manifestations of IgE-mediated (Type I) allergic reaction: urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm/wheeze, and anaphylaxis (hypotension/cardiovascular collapse). b) Antigenic component causing cross-reactivity between beta-lactams: the R1 side chain (not the shared beta-lactam ring/core) is the principal antigenic determinant responsible for cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins - cross-reactivity is best predicted by R1 side chain similarity, not by the class of drug itself. c) Prior SJS/TEN with penicillin: cephalosporins should generally be avoided, particularly any agent sharing a similar/identical R1 side chain, because skin testing has no predictive value in SJS/TEN and re-exposure risks a severe, life-threatening recurrence. A cephalosporin could only be considered if it has a distinctly different (dissimilar) R1 side chain with no structural relation to the culprit drug, and even then only with specialist (allergy) input and extreme caution - this drug should never be used as a de-labeling/challenge attempt.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 293-296 (R1 side chain cross-reactivity; SJS/TEN and skin testing limitations)

questions.question: What is: The mechanisms of penicillin. What pharmacodynamic principle applies to penicillin's mechanism. How would you optimize penicillin administration based on pharmacodynamics. What percent of skin tests are negative in patients reporting a penicillin allergy.

parts.text: The mechanism of penicillin
What pharmacodynamic principle applies
How would you optimize penicillin administration
What percent of skin tests are negative in patients reporting a penicillin allergy

cohort_answer.text: a) Binds PBP and prevents cross-linking of cell wall. b) Time over MIC dependent (t/MIC). c) Optimize dose such that time above MIC is optimized. d) >90%.

questions.question: Name the molecular target of each antifungal drug in the table.

parts.text: Posaconazole
Micafungin
Amphotericin
Terbinafine

questions.model_answer:
Posaconazole: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (fungal CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis.
Micafungin: (1,3)-beta-D-glucan synthase, blocking fungal cell wall glucan synthesis.
Amphotericin B: binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that disrupt membrane integrity.
Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase, blocking an earlier step of ergosterol synthesis.

questions.question: Pneumonia (inpatient, mild) in a pregnant woman with SJ to PCN.

parts.text: What is your treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides are safe for pregnancy. UpToDate suggests: Clindamycin plus aztreonam for mild CAP requiring admission with contraindication to cephalosporins. Short course of Moxifloxacin should be fine (author's opinion). If severe: Vancomycin, aztreonam and azithromycin. (ATS 2001; note - avoid all beta-lactams if Stevens-Johnson syndrome.)
